title: Dearer bread, poorer workers?
hook: Wheat got much dearer over 250 years. Did that make a working man poorer?

doesNotKnow: that a price rise says nothing about hardship until it is divided by pay
that a two-axis chart hides that division

misconception: When the price of bread rises over the centuries, people become poorer.
objective: The learner can say that from 1565 to 1810 wheat rose about 2.4 times but a mechanic's weekly wage rose 6 times, so a week's pay bought about 2.5 times as much wheat, and that dividing wage by price shows what a two-axis chart hides.

claims.text: The price of wheat (shillings per quarter) and the weekly wage of a good mechanic (shillings), every 5 years from 1565; wages stop at 1810.
claims.source: history-data.mjs: wheat, Wheat.csv, columns Year, Wheat, Wages (Playfair 1821 via HistData; 'a good mechanic' per the HistData doc). The 53 rows are copied into Demo.tsx unchanged; check section 7 of company/domains/briefs/checks/history-cycle1-check.mjs.

claims.text: From 1565 to 1810 the price of wheat rose about 2.4 times (41 to 99 shillings) and wages rose 6 times (5 to 30 shillings).
claims.source: 99 / 41 = 2.41; 30 / 5 = 6. Computed in Demo.tsx; history-cycle1-check.mjs section 7 '7 price and wage'.

claims.text: A week's pay bought 2.5 times as much wheat in 1810 as in 1565 (0.12 to 0.30 quarters).
claims.source: 5/41 = 0.122; 30/99 = 0.303; ratio 2.48, shown as 2.5. history-cycle1-check.mjs section 7 '7 wheat per week's wage'.

claims.text: On his own figures the best year for wages in wheat was 1785 (0.55 quarters a week), not the last one; the worst was 1595 (0.09).
claims.source: Max and min of Wages / Wheat over the rows with a wage: 1785, 23/42 = 0.548; 1595, 5.54/64 = 0.087. history-cycle1-check.mjs section 7 '7 best and worst'.

claims.text: Playfair drew price and wages on two different scales, which hides this ratio; dividing one by the other shows it as one line.
claims.source: HELD (the reveal's one held source sentence). Playfair (1821), A Letter on our Agricultural Distresses (public domain; not opened); the HistData Wheat doc (opened by cm-history) describes the chart. Fallback if not checkable: 'Drawn on two scales, price and wages hide this ratio' (no name). The stage's two-axis view is our re-draw from the data, not a trace of the original.

claims.text: Where it stops: this is one trade's wage and one food, not a cost of living.
claims.source: Brief 7 limit sentence: the file has one wage series ('a good mechanic') and one price (wheat), so it cannot be a cost-of-living index.

recall.question: Your pay doubles while rent triples. Can you afford more rent or less?
recall.why: What pay buys is pay divided by price: 2 / 3, about two-thirds as much rent.
